definition: Automated species identification is a method of making the expertise of taxonomists available to ecologists, parataxonomists and others via digital technology and artificial intelligence.
details: Today, most automated identification systems rely on images depicting the species for the identification. Based on precisely identified images of a species, a classifier is trained. Once exposed to a sufficient amount of training data, this classifier can then identify the trained species on previously unseen images.

explainer.lead: Automated species identification uses digital technology and artificial intelligence to recognize species, making taxonomic expertise available to ecologists, parataxonomists and others. Most systems identify species from images, allowing a trained classifier to suggest an identification for a new photograph.

tiers.eli5: It is like teaching a computer to recognize animals or plants from lots of correctly named photos. After enough practice, it can look at a new photo and name a species it has learned. This helps people who need taxonomic expertise but are not taxonomists themselves.
tiers.practitioner: A typical application trains an image classifier on precisely identified species images and then runs it on previously unseen images. Reliable reference labels and sufficient training data are essential. The classifier is limited to the species it was trained to identify.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a training set D = {(x_i, y_i)} of precisely identified images x_i and species labels y_i, learn a classifier f and predict y = f(x) for a previously unseen image. The method operationalizes taxonomic expertise as image-based classification. Its scope is constrained by the training data and the set of trained species.

explainer.example: Suppose precisely identified photographs of several butterfly species are used to train a classifier. When given a new photograph of one of those species, the classifier can identify it as that species.

usedIn.name: Ecology
usedIn.detail: Ecologists can use image-based classifiers to identify trained species.

usedIn.name: Parataxonomy
usedIn.detail: Parataxonomists can access taxonomic expertise through automated identification.

usedIn.name: Digital taxonomy
usedIn.detail: Precisely identified reference images provide the basis for training species classifiers.

explainer.intuition: A classifier learns visual patterns associated with each species from correctly identified examples. It can then apply that learned expertise to new images without requiring a taxonomist to examine every one.
howItWorks: Collect precisely identified images of the target species.
Train a classifier on those images and species labels.
Provide enough training data for the classifier to learn the distinctions.
Apply the trained classifier to previously unseen images.
Return an identification for a species included in training.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes taxonomic expertise accessible through digital tools rather than requiring every identification to be performed directly by a taxonomist. This supports ecologists, parataxonomists and others working with species images.
misconceptions: It cannot identify every possible species, only those covered by its training.
Training requires precisely identified images, not arbitrary unlabeled photographs.
It makes taxonomic expertise available digitally rather than defining taxonomy itself.

diagram.caption: Precisely identified images train a classifier that identifies trained species in new images.
